summary: The RSVP ASSOCIATION object links recovery label switched paths to the paths they protect in GMPLS. This informational RFC reviews how association is used in GMPLS recovery and defines no new procedures.

plainLanguage.summary: When a network operator builds a spare path to take over from a path that has failed, the two paths have to be linked so the routers know which is which. RFC 6689 explains how that link is read in GMPLS recovery signalling, and settles a long-running argument about it inside the IETF working group. It is a clarification only and changes no protocol.

subtitle: How the link between a working path and its recovery path is read in GMPLS recovery signalling.

tldr.problem: The ASSOCIATION object that links a recovery path to the path it protects had been read in different ways, and the working group kept asking which reading was right.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through the three fields of the object, then sorts the possible signalling orders into three cases and shows how a downstream router matches them. For end-to-end recovery it shows which cases each recovery type allows.
tldr.outcome: The document settles the argument without changing anything. It defines no new procedures, and where it differs from the two earlier RFCs it describes, those earlier documents remain authoritative.

today: RFC 6689 is an Informational RFC published in July 2012, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It clarifies how the ASSOCIATION object is read in RFC 4872 and RFC 4873, and says explicitly that where it differs from those documents they provide the authoritative text.

sections.title: Why This Document Exists
sections.content:
End-to-end recovery and segment recovery are defined for GMPLS-controlled label switched paths (LSPs) in RFC 4872 and RFC 4873. Both use the ASSOCIATION object to tie a recovery LSP to the LSP it protects. This RFC adds narrative on how those associations are to be recognised.

The reason for the document is history rather than design. Questions were repeatedly raised in the IETF's Common Control and Measurement Plane (CCAMP) working group about the right way to interpret the ASSOCIATION object in the context of end-to-end and segment recovery, and the group agreed that a document should be produced to close the matter. The text formalises an explanation that Adrian Farrel had given to the working group by email.

Nothing here changes the rules. The document defines no new procedures or mechanisms and is strictly informative in nature; where its wording and the text of RFC 4872 or RFC 4873 differ, the earlier documents provide the authoritative text.
sections.plainLanguage: When a network operator sets up a spare path to take over from a failed one, the two paths have to be linked so the routers know which is which. This RFC explains how that link is read and settles an argument about it. It changes nothing.

sections.title: The Link Object and Its Three Fields
sections.content:
Association works through the values carried in the ASSOCIATION object. That means association can happen independently of, and across, different RSVP-TE sessions, which is a significant step beyond what base MPLS or GMPLS allow. Association is always started by an upstream node, which inserts ASSOCIATION objects into the Path message of the LSPs that are to be associated; downstream nodes then correlate the LSPs they receive. The object has two class types, C-Type 1 and C-Type 2, with the same semantics and differing only in whether the address carried is IPv4 or IPv6.

Three fields do the work. The Association Type names the application and scopes the interpretation of the object; the values defined are Recovery and Resource Sharing, and the type has to match when two LSPs are matched. The Association Source gives the association a scope within the address space, and in the general case is the address of the node that originated the association. The Association ID is an identifier that further scopes the association; the rules for matching come from the Association Type, and the definition permits an arbitrary number of LSPs to be associated.

The object may only be carried in a Path message, so association happens based on Path state. More than one object may be present, which lets one LSP be associated in several ways at once: with one LSP for end-to-end recovery, with another for segment recovery, and with a third for resource sharing.
sections.plainLanguage: The link between a working path and its spare is carried in a small object that travels with the path's setup message. It has three parts: what kind of link it is, who created it, and an identifier. Routers downstream match these up to decide which paths belong together.

sections.title: End-to-End Recovery and Three Set-Up Orders
sections.content:
End-to-end recovery association takes one of two forms. Either several working LSPs share one recovery LSP, which matches the shared 1:N recovery type with N of one or more, or one working LSP has several recovery LSPs, which matches the other recovery types. Both forms use the same Association Type, Recovery, and the same Association Source: the tunnel sender address of the working LSP.

The Association ID may hold one of three values: the LSP ID of the LSP being protected, the LSP ID of the LSP protecting it, or, when the matching LSP is not yet known, the LSP ID of the LSP itself. The RFC then works through three signalling cases. In Case 1 the protected LSP is set up first, so every LSP in the group carries the protected LSP's LSP ID. In Case 2 the recovery LSP is set up first, so every LSP in the group carries the recovery LSP's LSP ID. In Case 3 both are set up at the same time, so the protected LSP carries the recovery LSP's LSP ID and the recovery LSP carries the protected LSP's LSP ID.

Case 3 is limited to end-to-end recovery, because it only applies to LSPs whose tunnel sender addresses match. Requirements elsewhere in RFC 4872 narrow the choice further. For the rerouting without extra traffic and shared mesh restoration types, and for the LSP rerouting type, the Association ID must be set to the primary working LSP's LSP ID, and that identifier must be known before the secondary LSP is signalled, so those types require Case 1 or Case 3 and exclude Case 2.
sections.plainLanguage: When a working path and its spare are set up, the identifier in the link can point at either one. The RFC sorts this into three cases depending on which path was created first, then shows which cases are allowed for each kind of recovery.

sections.title: Segment Recovery and Resource Sharing
sections.content:
Segment recovery reuses the association mechanism and the Association Type value from RFC 4872, but the processing and identification happen with respect to segment recovery LSPs. That means Case 2 is followed, the Association Source is the tunnel sender address of the segment recovery LSPs, and Case 3 does not apply. The RFC notes that the exclusion of Case 3 is not written out explicitly in RFC 4873, and suggests that spelling it out would have removed the need for this document.

Resource sharing, also defined in RFC 4873, is a different use of the same object. It lets LSPs with different SESSION objects share resources, which is not possible without the object. Because the Association Type is different, the semantics differ too. The type is set to Resource Sharing, the Association Source is set to the originating node's router address, and the Association ID is set to a value that uniquely identifies the set of LSPs to be associated. Setting that identifier to the working LSP's LSP ID is mentioned but only as a MAY, so the choice of identifier is left to the node that originates the association. All the LSPs in the group carry the identical ASSOCIATION object, which differs from recovery association, where the LSPs may carry different identifiers and still be associated.
sections.plainLanguage: Protecting part of a path rather than the whole path works differently: the spare path's address is the one recorded, and the third case is not allowed. Sharing the same fibre between paths is different again, and there all the paths carry exactly the same link object.

sections.title: How a Router Works Out That Two Paths Belong Together
sections.content:
Because the object only travels in Path messages, a receiver identifies associations from Path state alone, and it has to handle all three cases. Cases 1 and 2 are simple: the associated LSPs carry an identical ASSOCIATION object, and the same is true for resource sharing. A receiver compares all the fields of each ASSOCIATION object carried in the Path messages of each LSP, and treats the LSPs as associated when the same values appear in all fields of an object in each Path message. Since more than one association may exist, every carried object has to be examined.

Case 3 needs more work. For an ASSOCIATION object with the Association Type value Recovery that did not produce a match in that first comparison, the receiver looks for other LSPs with the same SESSION object fields and the same tunnel sender address fields as the LSP carrying the object. If such LSPs exist, it compares the Association ID with the LSP ID field of the other LSP, and identical values mean an end-to-end recovery association. Since this check only applies to end-to-end recovery, it need only be performed at the egress.

No extra behaviour is needed to support changes in the set of ASSOCIATION objects carried by an LSP, as long as a change is either a new association or a change of identifiers as described earlier.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that receives the setup message has to work out which paths belong together. It first compares the link objects field by field, which handles most cases. When that fails, it looks for paths with the same session and sender and checks whether the identifiers point at each other.

sections.title: Security and the Limits of This Document
sections.content:
The document reviews procedures that are defined in RFC 4872 and RFC 4873 and defines no new procedures of its own, so it introduces no new security considerations.

The same point about scope runs through the whole RFC. It is informative, it defines no new mechanism, and where its wording and the text of RFC 4872 or RFC 4873 differ, the earlier documents provide the authoritative text. The RFC also records that it was written in response to questions raised in the CCAMP working group by Nic Neate, and thanks Dimitri Papadimitriou, Francois Le Faucheur and Ashok Narayanan for comments and input.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC adds no security rules of its own, because it adds no rules at all. It is a clarification, and where it and the two earlier documents disagree, the earlier ones win.

viz.caption: THE THREE FIELDS OF THE ASSOCIATION OBJECT

items.title: Association Type
items.text: Names the application and scopes how the object is read. Recovery and Resource Sharing are defined.

items.title: Association Source
items.text: The address of the node that originated the association, giving the association its scope.

items.title: Association ID
items.text: An identifier that narrows the association further. The rules for matching come from the type.
